quote: the monster with the pointed tail
context: Virgil introduces him by what he does, not by name. The name comes only when Virgil gives him his orders, later in the canto.

note: No barrier keeps fraud out. It gets past mountains, city walls and armies, where force would fail.

Below this cliff lie the last two circles of Hell, which punish fraud: deceit of every kind, and at the very bottom, treachery. Dante counts fraud worse than violence because it misuses reason, the gift that sets humans apart (Canto 11).

quote: kept its tail hanging over the edge
note: The honest face is shown and the sting is kept out of sight. That is how fraud works.

quote: as gentle as a righteous man's
note: The three parts of the monster are the three stages of a swindle: a trustworthy face to win confidence, a patterned serpent's body for the twists of the scheme, and a poisoned tail for the harm done at the end.
Painted loops and small round shapes, like the pattern of a rich cloth. They are usually read as the snares of the deceiver and the covers that hide them.
The silks and carpets of Asia, brought west by merchants, were the most brilliant fabrics that Dante's Europe knew.

context: A weaver of webs is a fitting name beside the monster of fraud.

note: Medieval books of beasts said the beaver sat on the bank with its tail in the water and used it to lure or catch fish. Geryon sits the same way, with his weapon hanging behind him.
A stock insult. Italians of Dante's day spoke of the peoples north of the Alps as heavy eaters and drinkers. Beavers lived along their rivers.
The creature recalls the locusts of the Book of Revelation (chapter 9), which have human faces and tails that sting like scorpions.
Almost everywhere in Hell the poets turn to the left. They turn right only here and among the heretics' tombs (Inferno 9). No explanation has been generally accepted.
The usurers, moneylenders who charged interest. They are the last of the three groups on the burning sand, and sit at its very edge, right beside the pit of fraud.

Virgil explained in Canto 11 why lending at interest is violence against God. Humans are meant to live by nature and by their own work, which Dante calls art. The usurer makes money breed money and scorns both.
One of the very few times in Hell that Dante goes anywhere without Virgil. The usurers are not worth Virgil's time, and he does not speak a word to them or of them by name.

quote: Just as dogs do in summer
note: A deliberately low comparison. Men who were rich and proud in life are shown as dogs snapping at fleas.

Their faces tell him nothing, like those of the misers and spendthrifts in Canto 7. A life given to money has wiped out whatever made each one a person. Only the family crest on the purse says who he was.

quote: from each neck hung a pouch
note: A moneylender's purse, painted with his family's coat of arms. Arms were meant to proclaim a family's honor. Here they hang on moneybags, and the souls stare at them forever as they once stared at their profits.
A blue lion on a gold field: the arms of the Gianfigliazzi, a Florentine banking family of the Guelph party.
A white goose on a red field: the arms of the Obriachi, also called Ubriachi, a Florentine family of moneylenders on the Ghibelline side.

The arms of the Scrovegni of Padua. The speaker is usually identified as Reginaldo degli Scrovegni, who made a huge fortune by lending. His son Enrico built the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua, painted by Giotto about 1305, and it is often said he did so to atone for his father's usury.

A fellow Paduan who was still alive in 1300. He is usually identified as Vitaliano del Dente, a moneylender who later held high office in the city, though the identification is not certain. The damned are quick to announce who will be joining them.
Almost all the usurers here are from Florence, the banking capital of Europe. The city's wealth, Dante implies, is built on this sin.

Sarcasm. Early commentators identify him as Giovanni Buiamonte, a Florentine banker who was made a knight and was still alive in 1300. The damned of his own city are waiting for him as the prince of usurers.
His coat of arms. The Italian word, becchi, can mean goats or beaks, and the old commentators differ on which the arms showed.

quote: like an ox licking its nose
note: A coarse gesture of mockery, aimed at the men he has just named or at Dante. It is the last view Dante gives us of the usurers.

quote: This is how we descend from here
note: A sheer cliff separates the seventh circle from the eighth. There is no path or stair, so the only way down is on the monster's back.
The sense of the Italian is "I want to be in the middle": Virgil sits behind Dante, between him and the stinging tail.
A form of malaria, common in medieval Italy, in which the fever returns every fourth day. The attack begins with a fit of shivering, and the sufferer goes cold at the mere thought of it.
The first time the monster is named. Virgil has bargained with him out of Dante's hearing. Reason can make use of fraud's own strength, but keeps itself between Dante and the sting.
A living man with a real body, which has weight. Geryon is used to carrying nothing, or only shades.
The flight is described throughout as swimming and sailing. The thick dark air of Hell is treated as a kind of sea.

context: The scorch mark that "still shows" is the Milky Way, which one ancient story explained as the track his runaway chariot burned across the sky.
Both comparisons are of boys who flew and fell. Dante is flying too, but downward, under orders and held by his guide.

quote: by wind on my face and from below
note: A precise observation. In total darkness with nothing to see, the only sign of moving is the air: on the face from the forward motion, and from below from the descent.

context: The river of blood, which fell over the cliff at the end of Canto 16, crashes into a pool at the bottom.

quote: I saw fires and heard laments
context: Dante's first glimpse of the eighth circle, coming up at him out of the dark.

quote: Like a falcon long on the wing
note: From falconry, the sport of the medieval nobility. A hawk that has found no prey, and has not been called down by the lure, drops back to earth tired and sulking. Geryon is sullen in the same way: he came up expecting prey and got an errand.
Dante's Italian says "our persons". Only Dante has a body. Virgil is a shade.

quote: like an arrow from the string
note: After the slow, wide circles he was ordered to make, he is gone in an instant, glad to be rid of them.
